answer.rationale: With the contract expiring in 14 days and the line running at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, any switch of primary vendor or addition of a second source risks onboarding friction and delivery disruption exactly when there is no slack to absorb it. memory_c4 shows renegotiation at renewal previously recovered real margin and improved payment terms without changing the incumbent's service scope, and memory_c6 shows multi-year incumbent commitments unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service — together these suggest negotiating with the incumbent can plausibly meet the 18% cost mandate while preserving delivery continuity (also supported by memory_c1's stability record). I verified memory_c4 to confirm the renegotiation outcome was genuine margin recovery and not a one-off anecdote, and memory_c2 to check whether the low-cost vendor switch's onboarding-and-accuracy claims are robust enough to justify the higher-risk switch path instead — if that record shows hidden caveats, it strengthens the case against switching now. Renewing outright (memory_c1) doesn't address the cost mandate, deferring (memory_c5) was validated only for non-critical services and this is the primary constrained-capacity line, and switching or adding a source both introduce integration risk against a hard deadline and zero buffer. Negotiating terms is the action that directly targets cost without touching the fragile supply continuity.
